contributions.headingText: Paget disease of the penis and scrotum is a rare intraepidermal adenocarcinoma arising either as a primary tumour or by secondary involvement.
2C81.Y & XH70F8 Other specified malignant neoplasm of penis & Paget disease, extramammary

The tumour occurs in the epithelium and occasionally in the dermis of the penoscrotal region. Scrotal involvement is more common, with approximately half of the cases involving the scrotum only, one third involving both the scrotum and penis, and the remainder involving the penis alone {31650976; 31567917; 26508372; 18336601}.

Paget disease occurs in older men (age range: 42–91 years; reported median ages: 65–73 years) {31650976; 31567917; 28322288; 26508372; 18336601; 24731175}. Patients often have pruritus, erythema, pain, rash, erosion, and exudation {31650976; 26508372}. Most patients are initially misdiagnosed with a non-neoplastic disease. A median delay of 3–4 years has been reported from initial symptoms to the correct diagnosis {31650976; 28322288; 26508372; 18805708; 18336601; 24731175}.

Population frequencies have not been reported; however, there are recent large series from China and the USA {31650976; 31567917; 28322288}. In the 2004–2014 SEER registry, which covers approximately 28% of the population of the USA, 421 penoscrotal cases were reported {31567917}. Of these, 61% were in White people and 36% in people of Asian descent or Native Americans.

There are no known risk factors. Primary lesions are not HPV-associated {29745285}. Approximately 10% are secondary to a genitourinary malignancy, most frequently prostatic adenocarcinoma, followed by urothelial carcinoma {31567917}.

In primary Paget disease, a currently unidentified precursor cell gives rise to the tumour. Toker cells, potential precursor cells found in other regions, have not been identified in the penis or scrotum {31046904}. The cells giving rise to primary Paget disease may originate from apocrine glands, eccrine glands, or epidermal basal cells {31046904}. In secondary Paget disease, the cells arise from direct extension of an underlying tumour or from epidermotropic spread, usually urogenital, colorectal, or cutaneous in origin. Typically, metastatic lesions are metachronous rather than synchronous, presenting at a median interval of 4 years {31567917}.
Lesions are erythematous and scaly, with possible ulceration and exudation. They generally cover a large area (median: 20.5 cm2) {31650976}.

Paget cells occur singly or in small clusters in the epidermis (in situ), whereas 10–20% have invasive tumour cells within the dermis {31650976; 28322288}. Infiltration of the dartos muscle of the scrotum may be seen {26508372}. Tumour cells are round with abundant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, large nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Not infrequently, Paget cells involve sweat glands and hair follicles. An in situ tumour can form glandular structures {26508372}. An invasive tumour can form nodules, glands, or sheets {26508372}. Hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis are frequently present, and the upper dermis can have dense inflammation. Lymphovascular invasion is not infrequent. Perineural invasion is uncommon {26508372}.

Cells in primary Paget disease are reported to express CK7 and CEA, with variable expression of ERBB2 and GCDFP-15. HMB45, S100, CK20, vimentin, CDX2, and HPV are usually negative or focally positive {31650976; 26508372; 29745285}. Immunohistochemistry in secondary disease is similar to that of the underlying carcinoma type.

Essential: single and/or clusters of atypical intraepithelial cells positive for CK7 and negative for CK20 and melanocytic markers.

Desirable: correlation with clinical history; evaluation of expression of possible secondary malignancies.

Lesions are treated with wide local excision or Mohs micrographic surgery. Resection is associated with improved survival {31650976; 31046904; 28178005; 31567917; 29636019}. Potential risk factors for progression include younger age, shorter symptom duration, delay in diagnosis, exudation, elevated serum CEA, adnexal involvement, depth of invasion, wide horizontal invasion, nodule formation, marked inflammation, lymphovascular invasion, and ERBB2 and p53 expression {31650976; 28322288; 26508372; 19438449}. Recurrence is reported in 10–40% of cases {28322288; 26508372; 18336601}. The most frequent metastatic sites are regional inguinal lymph nodes. Non-regional lymph nodes and bone are the most common distant metastatic sites {19438449; 18805708; 24731175}. Lymph node metastasis is seen in 5–34% of patients {28322288; 26508372; 18805708}. Overall 3- to 5-year survival is approximately 70% {31567917; 26508372; 28322288; 24731175}.
